title: Audit logging: add coverage scanner job + CI gate for sensitive-action inventory
author: Sahana Iyer
body:
Context: As part of audit log schema v1 + instrumentation, we need an enforceable definition of “100% coverage for sensitive actions.” This PR adds an automated coverage scanner that compares the sensitive action inventory against the audit-event registry and schema-v1 validators, and wires it into CI as a gate for changes to the inventory and event registry. The scanner produces a human-readable coverage summary in build output and emits a machine-readable artifact used by the coverage dashboard job.

What this adds: (1) A new `audit-coverage-scan` job (runs in CI and can also be invoked locally) (2) Coverage rules: every sensitive action must map to >=1 registered event name; every mapped event must exist in the registry; every event used for sensitive actions must be schema-v1 validated; inventory rows must include an owner (team/service) and subsystem tag (api/console/rbac/dedicated/private/etc.) (3) A strict gate: PRs that modify the sensitive action inventory or audit event registry will fail CI if coverage decreases OR if there are unmapped/unknown event names; an escape hatch exists via `audit_coverage_exceptions.yaml` with a required expiration date and Security approval note (4) Output: coverage % by subsystem and a list of missing mappings, unknown events, and “registered but not validated” events printed to build output, plus JSON artifact `audit_coverage_report.json` uploaded by CI.

Why this approach: inventory-first means we can block new sensitive actions from landing without audit coverage, while allowing existing gaps to be tracked and burned down. This is intentionally not sampling-based; audit logs must be deterministic and complete.

Implementation notes: Inventory is read from `security/audit-logging/sensitive_actions_inventory.yaml` (the Confluence table will remain the source of truth for humans; this YAML is the versioned build input). The scanner reads the audit-event registry generated by `audit/events/registry.ts` and ensures each mapped event name is present. Schema validation coverage is checked by ensuring the emitting client uses the shared `AuditEventV1` types (for TS services) or calls `audit.validateV1()` (for Go services), and by verifying the event is included in the pipeline validator allowlist. We keep these checks intentionally conservative; if the scanner can’t prove an event is validated, it fails with remediation guidance.

Developer workflow: Run `./bin/audit-coverage scan` locally to see the same report as CI. When adding a sensitive action: add an inventory row with a stable `action_id`, owner, subsystem, and `expected_events`; ensure each event is registered; ensure the service emits and validates schema-v1.

Example CI output:
- Overall coverage: 78% (baseline 78%, no regression)
- api: 81% (23/28) missing: api.keys.rotate (expected: api.api_key.rotated)
- rbac: 75% (12/16) missing: rbac.roles.permission_change (expected: rbac.role.permissions.updated)
- dedicated: 67% (6/9) missing: dedicated.capacity.quota_update
- private: 80% (8/10) missing: private.upgrade.rollback

Rollout: Gate is “no regressions” for existing inventory; for new sensitive actions added in a PR, full mapping/registry/validation is required. A follow-up will turn on “must be 100%” once instrumentation catches up (tracked in ENG-2491).

Risk: Potential false positives if we can’t statically detect schema validation in some services. Mitigations: (a) explicit allowlist with justification, (b) clearer conventions for validation calls, (c) scanner only gates when inventory/registry changes (not on unrelated PRs).

Testing: unit tests for parsing inventory + registry resolution + rule evaluation; CI dry-run in `audit-coverage-scan` with a fixture repo layout; added a regression test for unknown event names.

Docs: updated in-repo developer guidance with “how to add a sensitive action” checklist and examples.

Notes: This does not replace runtime validation in the audit-log pipeline; it ensures engineering cannot introduce new sensitive actions without a corresponding audit event surface.
commits: audit-coverage: initial scanner CLI + report format
audit-coverage: add inventory parser + mapping rules
ci: wire audit-coverage-scan into PR checks (only on inventory/registry diffs)
audit-coverage: add exceptions file format + expiry enforcement
docs: add developer checklist + troubleshooting section
tests: add fixtures + regression for unknown event names
review_conversation: Mei Lin: Love the direction. Can we ensure the report artifact includes per-subsystem counts so the dashboard job doesn’t have to re-parse the human output?
Sahana Iyer (author): Yep — added `subsystems: {name, total, covered, missing_action_ids}` to `audit_coverage_report.json` and updated the dashboard consumer stub.
Nadia Rahman: Two questions: (1) why gate only when inventory/registry changes? (2) will this miss a service adding a new sensitive action code path without updating inventory?

Sahana Iyer (author): (1) to avoid flakiness/false positives blocking unrelated work while we stabilize detection logic; (2) yes, inventory discipline is the assumption — the companion policy doc will require inventory updates for sensitive-action additions; once stabilized we can expand gating to directories that commonly add sensitive actions (auth/rbac/api-keys/controllers).
Marcus Lin: Exception file needs stronger guardrails: require an expiry AND a Security review reference. Also please ensure exceptions cannot be wildcarded.
Sahana Iyer (author): Done. Exceptions now require `expires_at` (max 30 days) and `security_review` text; event names must be explicit (no '*' or regex). Added tests.

Allison Grant: Naming: the job is `audit-coverage-scan` but the CLI is `audit-coverage`. Can we standardize to `audit-coverage` everywhere? Also please include a link to the runbook/standards doc in CI output.
Sahana Iyer (author): Standardized to `audit-coverage` for both. CI output now prints a short help block + link to `docs/engineering/audit-logging/coverage.md`.
Mei Lin: Approve once the baseline behavior is clear: if overall baseline is 78%, do we fail if a subsystem drops but overall stays same?
Sahana Iyer (author): We fail on any subsystem regression OR overall regression. Implemented by comparing against `main` artifact when the workflow runs on PRs touching inventory/registry.
